strengths: The task addresses a meaningful gap between audio-visual semantic segmentation and video instance segmentation: distinguishing individual sounding objects, including instances of the same class, and maintaining their identities over time. Figure 1 clearly illustrates this distinction, with plausible applications in video editing and multimodal understanding.

AVISeg represents concrete annotation work: 117 annotated videos containing 6,973 frames, 281 objects, and 15,355 masks. The broader collection spans 26 categories and five scenarios, with an average duration of 62.6 seconds, offering a useful direction for studying longer audio-visual interactions.

The baseline combines established components—Mask2Former, VGGish, TPAVI, and audio-conditioned queries—in a plausible framework. Table 1 reports 31.5 AP with ResNet-50 and 35.6 AP with Swin-Base, providing initial feasibility evidence. The standard spatiotemporal IoU and AP/AR metrics appropriately evaluate instance tracks, and several training settings are explicitly documented.
weaknesses: The central experimental gap is whether audio determines which instances are segmented. Table 1 compares only visual backbones; there is no visual-only baseline, muted/shuffled-audio control, or ablation of fusion and audio-conditioned queries. Consequently, the results cannot establish sound-dependent source selection beyond visual category and motion cues. Together with the annotation uncertainties below, this insufficient validation of the central contribution determines my weak-reject recommendation.

The evaluated benchmark is insufficiently characterized. Only 117 of the 1,258 collected videos are annotated, split into 84 training and 33 testing videos. Figure 3 describes the broader collection, while category and scenario distributions for the labeled splits are not reported. Neither the prevalence of competing same-class sound sources nor performance on changing audible intervals is quantified. These omissions make it difficult to assess whether the reported aggregate AP meaningfully covers the task's distinctive challenges; the modest dataset size alone is not the decisive concern.

Ground-truth validity needs stronger support. Section 3 describes SAM-assisted annotation and calls the annotations high quality, but does not explain how annotators attribute overlapping sounds to specific objects, determine audible intervals, preserve identities through silence, or verify annotation quality. SAM-assisted spatial masks do not establish correct sound-source attribution. The single interval notation in Section 4.1 also leaves handling of repeated, discontinuous sounding intervals unclear.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Equation (1) does not specify the tensor contractions and projections needed to interpret its residual addition. The time-indexed learnable instance queries are not clearly reconciled with training on two frames and inference on variable-length videos. Audio-window alignment and pretrained initialization are also unspecified, and the manuscript provides no access information for the dataset or implementation. These gaps limit independent reproduction and technical verification.

A secondary presentation issue is that Section 5.2 describes Figure 6 as raw-frame, ground-truth, and prediction columns, whereas the displayed figure uses temporal columns and paired rows. This is readily correctable and does not drive the recommendation.
